Now, cause and effect are illusory phenomena used to grasp the principle; once the principle is attained, the phenomena vanish. Rationality (tattva) is a provisional name used to realize the truth;
once realization is attained, the name vanishes. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he did not apprehend a single dharma as real;
with an empty fist, he deceived small children to entice and deliver all beings."
It is solely due to the presence or absence of wisdom that intimacy and distance cause delusion to become thick or thin.

The previous statement regarding "extinguishing" (wan) merely uses this as a provisional means to manifest the principle; one must know that the wisdom of extinction permeates both the beginning and the end.

It is simply because of intimacy and distance that one proceeds through stages according to merit—just as the six stages of "extinction" (wan) are followed by the five stages of "wisdom" (zhi). Therefore, it is precisely because of the wisdom of extinction that [the subsequent stages arise].
The division into five [stages] is based precisely on the distinction between the immediate (*pratyakṣa*) and the remote (*parokṣa*).

Other commentators claim that only the first stage is considered immediate while the "similar" stage is considered remote, and further assign these categories of immediacy and remoteness to the sharp and dull faculties respectively; however, this is incorrect. Since the meaning of the subsequent text opens up six stages within the "six identities," how could it stop at merely dividing the "true" stage?
Furthermore, how could the three delusions possibly be related to sharp or dull faculties? This classification is made solely with respect to the five [stages] within a single person.
Thus, discussing the relative closeness and distance [of these delusions] is inherently consistent with the principle.
Because they are confused regarding their density or thinness, one forcibly distinguishes them as the three delusions.

When a person of the Perfect Teaching first takes the true aspect (*dharmatā*) as their object, the境 (object) is immediately the Middle; it is "severing without severing," for they fundamentally sever ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because the two delusions are spontaneously eliminated first, it is said that "the first stage of faith eliminates the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while the seventh stage of faith eliminates the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*)," and so forth.
In reality, however, the essence of both views and thought is ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the *Wénjù* (Text on Words and Phrases) states:

"The principle of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is defiled by the two delusions—the general and the specific—and is therefore difficult to comprehend. The commentary (*Jì*) explains: "Because these two delusions cannot be distinguished [as separate entities], it is said to be 'difficult'."
The statement that "the present [teaching] is forcibly divided" arises precisely from this.
In terms of meaning, it opens into six stages of identity (*liu ji*).

The *Record* states: "In terms of principle (*li*), the realized Dharma has no name; in terms of phenomena (*shi*), the various stages are not non-existent. The present statement refers to this meaning.
The opening of the six [identities] is precisely its intended meaning.
The names refer to the shallowness or depth of wisdom;
"intimacy" and "remoteness" follow the shallowness or depth of practice according to the stages.
Therefore, one knows that through diligent application, empty names and delusions are severed.
By diligently applying the three wisdoms, the three delusions are extinguished. Another commentary cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states:

"Emptiness has only a name but lacks reality; delusion is likewise the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and thus has only a name. Thus, the name "emptiness" is employed as a metaphor for the falsity of delusion.
When the cause of illusion is fulfilled, the fruit of the mirror-image is perfected.
Since the stages of cause and effect are pervasive, they are described as "perfectly complete.

Regarding the four metaphors cited—dream, space, illusion, and image—the first three illustrate that the substance [of phenomena] cannot be apprehended, while the last one illustrates that which appears spontaneously.
Although "emptiness" (*śūnya*) and "image" (*pratibimba*) are identical in meaning, emptiness is void while an image is substantial.
Although they are alike in being empty, emptiness has no form whereas an image can be seen; thus, in relation to emptiness, the image is further termed "substantial."
Because it is real, it is said that principle is fundamentally present;
as an analogy, when the fruit of the three thousand [dharmas] is perfected, they immediately manifest.
Because it is empty and void, delusion turns back to become the true nature.
This is illustrated by the transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, it changes into clarity (*vidyā*). The reading "nature is established" (*xing cheng*) in other editions is an error.
This is the non-duality within duality that establishes the distinction between cause and effect; yet, though dual, it is non-dual, for the essence is one from beginning to end.
If one were to claim that the cause differs from the effect, then the cause would not truly be a cause.
Because the causal conditions are not complete, this is not a perfect cause.
One must understand that the fruit arises from the cause, and only then can the fruit be realized;
the fruit relies upon perfect cultivation to attain the sublime result.
Therefore, the three thousand [dharmas] existing within principle are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

Within principle, the three thousand dharmas of the fruition-virtue are termed the "three paths": the *dharmakāya* is suffering (*duḥkha*), *prajñā* is affliction (*kleśa*), and liberation (*vimukti*) is karma (*karman*).
Here, for brevity, we speak only of affliction. Furthermore, ignorance is the root of non-abiding, while karma and suffering are its manifestations.
The principle established here is that what exists now is said to reside within the fundamental reality (*li*); this is because by citing the root, the branches are encompassed.
When the three thousand phenomena are perfected as the fruit, they are all termed "Eternal" and "Blissful.

The three thousand phenomena of the causal principle, upon reaching the fruit, are termed the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*): suffering becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), delusion becomes Prajñā, and karma becomes [the Enjoyment-body].
Liberation possesses all four virtues, which are here briefly stated as two. Furthermore, "permanence" and "bliss" belong to the Dharma-body;
"purity" belongs to Prajñā; and "self" belongs to liberation. Here, by speaking of the "accomplishment of the fruit," the entire essence is shown to encompass its functions.
"The three thousand [realms] are unchanging; ignorance is itself enlightenment.
This explains the preceding phrase: because the dharma-nature of the three thousand realms remains unaltered as it follows conditions, it is said to be "unchanging.
The three thousand are simultaneously eternal, both in essence and in function.

The latter phrase is explained as follows: because the three thousand [realms] are entirely the substance of the Dharmakāya and the function of the two natures (dharmas), it is said that they are "both eternal.
This is merely an abbreviation.
This is established through the Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature.

Question: The previous section on "Cultivating Nature" (*xiuxing*) was said to encompass both wisdom (*zhi*) and practice (*xing*), with wisdom corresponding to the stages prior to the [first] abiding (*zhuzhuan*) and practice corresponding to the three [subsequent] abidings. Now, however, you state that cultivating nature is the cause. Since the cause should belong to the stages prior to abiding and the fruit belongs to the first abiding, why does this section speak of the "perfection of the cause" and the "fullness of the fruit"? Answer: The Record states: The cultivation of nature is the cause; because the cause is established, the resultant fruit is named. Regarding the previous section on cultivating nature, it was taught that it encompasses both wisdom and practice. Wisdom corresponds to the stages prior to the first abiding, while practice corresponds to the three subsequent abidings. Now, by taking the cultivation of nature as the cause, the cause indeed belongs to the stages prior to abiding, and the fruit resides in the first abiding. Why, then, is there here the teaching of the perfection of the cause and the fullness of the fruit? The Record explains: "The cause is the cultivation of nature; the fruit is the manifestation of the Dharma-body. Because the cause is perfected, the fruit is fully realized.

The 'perfection of the cause' refers to the fulfillment of the causal practices within the stages prior to abiding; the 'fullness of the fruit' refers to the attainment of the ultimate fruit within the first abiding. Thus, although the substance of the cause and fruit are distinct, their essence is non-dual. This is why they are spoken of together."* *(Note: The text provided in the prompt appears to be a commentary on a specific doctrinal point regarding the relationship between cause and fruit in the context of the Tiantai or Huayan scholastic systems.)*

Now, since it is said that practitioners mostly reside in the stage prior to the first abode (*zhùqián*), we know that what is being addressed is merely a provisional indication. Furthermore, the Record states:

"If one reaches the first abode, it is called the 'fruit according to one's portion' (*suífēnguǒ*)," and it also says: "The three—object, wisdom, and practice—pass through the six successive stages until they reach the fruit.
Therefore, we know that those who claim the "fruit" refers exclusively to the first abode are being far too restrictive.

Regarding the fifth gate, the non-duality of defilement and purity: if one realizes that from time immemorial the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is itself ignorance, then one can understand that what is now ignorance is itself the *dharmatā*.
To clarify the dependent origination of defilement and purity, this first demonstrates the fundamental basis of beginninglessness and non-abiding. The *Commentary* states: "The *dharmatā*..."
Thus, the dharma-nature of ignorance has no abiding place; ignorance itself is dharma-nature, and ignorance has no abiding place.
Although both the dharma-nature of ignorance and ignorance itself have no abiding place, they serve as the root of all dharmas.
Since this now demonstrates the essence of contemplation, one must therefore realize that ignorance is identical to dharma-nature, taking dharma-nature as the root. If one understands this...
According to this fundamental principle, all dharmas of defilement and purity established herein depend upon the moment (kṣaṇa).
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) together with ignorance (avidyā), which universally produce all dharmas, is termed "defilement."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā), following the conditions of ignorance, truly creates the nine realms; as all these are the flowing and revolving of the three paths, they are termed "defiled.

Regarding the term "conjoined" (*yu*), the *Dilun* states: "Only the True does not give birth, and solitary delusion cannot be established; it is through the union of the True and the delusive that there is anything accomplished.
Furthermore, even for a person of the Perfect Teaching who has not yet shattered ignorance, although they have returned [to the source], they still create the Buddha-realm.
It is called "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) because it clarifies that the pure dharmas apply only after the fruit has been attained;

thus, in the *Wénjù jì* (Commentary on the Text), within the section explaining the provisional and real aspects of phenomena and principle, it states: "The mind, consciousness, and awareness, as well as pure and impure karma, are established as all dharmas through defiled conditions.

Furthermore, within the section explaining the provisional and real aspects of essence and function, it states: "The function of the hundred realms belonging to the partial fruit of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is [the application]."

Regarding the establishment of all phenomena based on pure conditions, the text itself refers to this as being clarified in the *Ran-jing bu-er men* (The Gate of the Non-duality of Defilement and Purity):
"Ignorance and the dharma-nature universally respond to various conditions; they are designated as 'pure.'"
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) induced by ignorance should provisionally create the ten realms; as these are all the most excellent functions within the fruit, they are called "pure.

They are also referred to as "bestowing" (*yǔ*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) clarifies that what is created through the transformations of the sages also causes sentient beings to transform their minds so that they perceive [the realm].
Furthermore, the *Fuxing* states: "In one's own practice, transformation arises from observing the conditions of defilement; in transforming others, however, it is by means of..."
Regarding the arising through pure causes and conditions in the mutual relationship between self and others, it arises from the combined causes and conditions of defilement and purity.

Since it is stated here that [the mind] "universally responds to all conditions," this precisely refers to the combination of defilement and purity; thus, one knows that the character "and" (yǔ) cannot be omitted.
As for the absence of these two instances of the character "and" in other editions, it is likely that former readers, not being well-versed in its meaning, arbitrarily removed them.
This is merely a matter of excision.
Whether turbid water or clear water, there is no difference in their being moistened by waves;
though clarity and turbidity arise from conditions, both types of water produce two kinds of waves because of the wind. Likewise, the two natures of defilement and purity both arise from delusion.
Therefore, the two functions arise,
and turbidity becomes inherently present.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have possessed nothing but afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Although turbidity is inherently present, its entire substance is pure.
The three paths are entirely the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of the three causes.

Because the principle of the two waves universally indicates that the substance is itself the function, the three thousand [realms] of cause and effect are both termed the "dependent origination of delusion and enlightenment."
Dependent origination is not separate from the moment.

Just as turbid water and clear water are indistinguishable in their waves and moisture when combined, this inclusion of phenomena within principle shows that there is no reason to claim the moment is not real but rather false.
The principle that momentariness and dependent origination are one is the same as the aforementioned two waves;
the principle that the whole substance is function applies universally here, indicating that the principle is fused with phenomena.
However, once the first and last [extremes] are joined, the middle becomes self-evident.
Within the single principle, one distinguishes between the pure and the defiled;
that is, within the single principle of dependent origination, one distinguishes the characteristics of pure and defiled dependent origination.
Specifically, there are six defilements and four purities.
This statement refers to the ten realms as distinct categories.
Generally speaking, however, these ten realms encompass both the pure and the impure;
this refers to the mutual inclusion of the ten realms. This is as when Zhanran asked why the ten realms possess one another as their causes.

Regarding the answer concerning the mutual presence of cause and fruit: it is difficult to manifest the cause when there is a separation between them, whereas it is easy to know the pervasive nature of the cause.

For example, as the Maiden Maitrāyaṇī developed the Buddha-mind toward the hell realm, others explained that when the ten realms are viewed in relation to one another, the hell realm is exclusively defiled and the Buddha realm is exclusively pure.

Among the intermediate eight realms, when viewed from below, they are pure; when viewed from above, they are defiled. Since they thus mutually possess both purity and defilement, [the relationship of cause and fruit is established].
Therefore, it is named "pervasive" (*tong*); although its actual substance consists of eight pervasive [realms], they are collectively referred to as ten.

Thus we know that the meaning of "pervasiveness" is precisely what is intended here by the text regarding defilement and purity: only the Buddha-realm is called pure, while the other nine are equally pervasive of both defilement and purity.

Now, if this were the case, one should simply say that, in terms of distinction, nine are defiled and one is pure; whereas in terms of pervasiveness, all ten are pervasive of both purity and defilement. This is because—
Since "defiled and pure" is identical to "pure and defiled," it is by way of contrast that the distinct meaning is revealed; this is precisely the intended sense here.

One should know that "defiled and pure" is spoken of in terms of the essence and function of delusion and enlightenment, while "pure and defiled" is distinguished according to the realm-like nature (*dharmatā*) of ordinary beings and sages.

When in a state of delusion, ignorance serves as the essence and the creation of the nine realms serves as the function; thus, both the pure and defiled realms and their *dharmatā* are entirely defiled.
Awakening takes the dharma-nature as its essence and the ten practices as its function; thus, both pure and impure realms are entirely purified.
Therefore, one knows that the defiled essence of each moment is entirely pure.
Since one realizes that the ten [practices] pervade both the pure and the impure, one knows that the defiled essence of ignorance in each moment is identical to the dharma of the sages.

The essence of intrinsic purity is spontaneously endowed with the ten realms by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); thus, when "a single moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is mentioned, it refers to the most brief instant of thought.
As the *Mohe zhiguan* states: "It is simply a state of no-mind; yet as soon as there is even a slight stirring of mind, the three thousand [realms] are immediately present."
The three thousand realms have not yet been manifested and verified, so their essence remains obscure;
because the afflictions of views and thoughts have not yet been shattered, they specifically receive the name "obscure. The *Erya* states that "reng" (仍) means "yin" (因), or cause.
Thus, in the stage of semblance, the six faculties achieve universal illumination.
From the seventh stage of faith upward, because the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is endowed with the five eyes, it is able to universally illumine the ten realms;

this is likewise true even for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). Question: How does the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) universally illumine? Answer: The forms and images of the ten realms all manifest within the body;

furthermore, through the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation (*samanta-mukha-samādhi*), one transforms and appears throughout the ten realms—this is its characteristic. One should know that the six faculties are thus pervasive.

In "Illumination," the meaning of the ten [realms] being complete within both cause and fruit is clearly manifested. Zhanran’s statement that "the cause is pervasive while the fruit is distinct" refers specifically to the first three [of the ten realms].
In "Illumination," it is evident that each of the ten realms possesses [the others] in its entirety.

Since illumination appears as if it were the true [realm], ten must necessarily become one hundred realms; furthermore, by encompassing both the provisional and the real, the three thousand realms arise spontaneously.
Please observe that each possesses [the others]—this is evident when examining how the ten realms pervade both the pure and the impure.
How could those with the six sense organs purified claim that the ten realms are fixed as ten?

Since the text of the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" has not yet explicitly shown the characteristics of the mutual inclusion of the ten realms, there is a fear that people might definitively conclude [otherwise];
therefore, this is explained here.
The same applies to the partial realization (divisions of truth) and the manifestation of traces across the ten realms.
The "similar pervasive illumination" still belongs to the cultivation based on conditions;

from the first stage upward, when the essence of true cultivation is manifested, one realizes the fundamental Dharma-body and extends traces throughout the ten realms—this is termed the "inconceivable response."
Up until the attainment of the fruit, it is equal to those hundred realms.
When the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is attained, there is nothing further revealed; it is simply that its ultimate nature is coextensive with the fundamental reality of those hundred realms.
(The reading "乃由果成" [attained by virtue of the fruit] in earlier editions is an erroneous interpretation; some commentators explain this as being due to the partial realization of the Buddha-fruit.)
Regarding the ability to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment within a hundred worlds: even if we grant that there are a hundred worlds, how can this be so?
Is it not because the preceding text stated that the three thousandfold world-system has not yet been clearly verified and its essence remains obscure?

Therefore, it is known that by referring to the stage of "semblance" (sādharmya) and below, the manifestation of the essence is clarified; thus, to claim equality with that [stage] must refer back to the preceding text. Moreover, within the stage of semblance, it is said that there is "illumination."
To divide each of the ten realms into ten is merely to illuminate the characteristics of the preceding hundred realms.

Furthermore, the passage below states that "the three dharmas are simply the realization of that principle, and the attainment of the Way within the three hundred realms is surely not the intended meaning here."
Therefore, from the very first moment of the mind, one must both negate and illumine.
Although the hundred realms manifested thereby may be traced back to higher stages, the essential point of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) lies in this initial moment of illumination.
Because of this illumination, the three thousand realms are eternally present; because of this negation, they are naturally empty.
The three thousand realms are provisional, while emptiness is the reality; this is precisely the "true aspect of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Since the true aspect necessarily comprises all phenomena, it is said that they are "constantly endowed with all phenomena"; since all phenomena are necessarily the true aspect, it is said that this is "the natural law" (*dharmatā*). This reveals that the three contemplations are simultaneous. Question:

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of our school, the two truths are most often defined such that the conventional consists of emptiness and the provisional, while the Middle Way constitutes the ultimate truth.
Question: Why is it that the provisional and the real are further distinguished such that the conventional dharma is taken as the provisional and emptiness as the real? Answer:

The true and the conventional are distinguished in terms of the middle and the extremes, while the provisional and the real are divided in terms of phenomena and principle. One should know that regarding emptiness in relation to the Middle Way:

since the Middle is free from all dependence, emptiness still stands in contrast to the conventional; therefore, it belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). However, when viewed in relation to provisional dharmas, the provisional is established [by means of emptiness].

Because the emptiness established by means of conceptualization must be extinguished and eliminated, it belongs to the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Thus, the essence of inconceivable emptiness is itself the Middle Way;
however, because its names and meanings involve the process of cultivation and realization, it is categorized as conventional.
Throughout the day there is the simultaneous negation of both, and throughout the day there is the simultaneous illumination of both.

Furthermore, this negation of the preceding [negation] and the illumination of the preceding [illumination] also reveals their simultaneity; thus it is said, "throughout the day. As the *Wenju* states:

"It is not emptiness, provisional existence, or the Middle Way, yet it illuminates emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way. Furthermore, as the *Zhi guan* states: "It is not three, yet..."
The "three threes" do not constitute three; rather, through their mutual spacing, they form the wondrous. Instances of this are not limited to one.
Without moving from this single thought, one responds universally to all directions.

The substance of this thought is vast and pervasive throughout the ten realms and penetrates the three periods of time; how could the universal response on the level of fruition not be derived from this?
The *Yi* says, "The spirit has no fixed location, and the *yi* has no fixed form. Kangbo said: It cannot be understood through a single direction or a single form.
Responding to stimuli as they arise, purity and impurity both vanish.
Giving should proceed by means of illumination to dissolve appearances through negation;
because purity and impurity have vanished, one relies on emptiness and the Middle Way. Yet, within emptiness and the Middle Way, one transforms defilement into purity.
These two contemplations of emptiness and the Middle Way do not merely cause the disappearance of the phenomena created, but also transform the creator itself.
In its essence, what is it that ignorance does not turn away from within emptiness? What is it that the *dharmatā* does not manifest within emptiness?
It is not merely that the essence of ignorance and the essence of *dharmatā* are non-dual; for if both are observed as empty, then ignorance itself is [the *dharmatā*].

If ignorance is not itself, how can delusion be transformed into wisdom? How can the defiled be turned into the pure? One might ask: "The perfect destruction of ignorance should pertain only to the Middle Way. Why is this so?
Using emptiness to respond to emptiness is the function of the Middle Way; being within the Middle Way is the essence of the contemplation of emptiness.
If there were no Middle Way within emptiness, it would not differ from the partial truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*); if the Middle Way were not empty, how could it dispel all marks?

Therefore, the reason why various texts state that the contemplation of the Middle Way clearly reveals the two kinds of emptiness—the emptiness of arising and the emptiness of phenomena—is precisely because of this. Question: What is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*)?

The answer is that there is no transformation of defilement into purity. To provisionally refute the "dusts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," these sands represent obstacles to phenomena (*dharmas*) and belong to the practice of transforming others (*parārtha*), not one's own practice (*svārtha*).

As for the delusions regarding the principle (*tattva*), in reality, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are cultivated within a single mind; however, when discussed individually, they are therefore categorized as only two.
Because defilement and purity are understood as being within emptiness, they vanish of themselves.

The perfection of abandonment constitutes the perfection of wisdom; since the former clarifies the aspect of vanishing, it speaks of "purity," while the latter clarifies the sense of transformation, thus speaking of "defilement and purity.
If one were to claim they are identical, why would the text reverse their order?
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect.

By contemplating the essence of defilement as the cause, one attains the function of purity as the fruit; while the former pertains to one's own practice, this encompasses the transformation of others.
Sixth is the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*): having already realized that the *dharmadhātu* and the single substance are non-dual.

The dwelling place of the Dharma-body is called the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (Nityapraśāntaprakāśa). The Dharma-body does not have the form of the aggregates (skandha) or sense bases (āyatana), and the Quiescent Light has no marks of adornment.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "True Suchness and Buddha-nature are neither body nor land, yet they are spoken of as body and land;

apart from the body there is no land, and apart from the land there is no body. To speak of "body and land" refers to one phenomenon with two meanings; here, we cite it to negate [dualistic distinctions].
Since that body necessarily incorporates the land, it is called "the one body, non-dual. How much more so for Vairocana, who pervades all places;
one should know that there are no dharmas whatsoever that are not the Buddha-dharma. As the *Golden Needle* states:

"When a single Buddha attains enlightenment, throughout the entire dharma-realm there is nothing that is not the non-dual unity of this Buddha’s environment and its inhabitants. This is precisely the meaning of this principle.
This is truly because the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment from time immemorial are equal to those hundred worlds;
for among these three thousand, two thousand belong to the mental aggregates (*skandha*) as the primary realm, while one thousand belong to the environment as the supporting basis.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* establishes three kinds of worlds: the world of sentient beings, the world of dwelling places, and the world of the five aggregates.
The world of sentient beings refers to the provisional designation of names and the false conception of a sovereign master within the actual phenomena of the five aggregates.
Among the ten realms—whether ordinary or sagely—all without exception rely upon these three kinds of worlds to create the ten "suchnesses" (*yathābhūta*).

Since the environment and its inhabitants both reside within the one mind, how could the one mind be divided into subject and object? Although there is no subject or object, the environment and its inhabitants remain distinct.
The body and land of Vairocana are like a mirror and a vessel, while the three thousand worlds of the environment and its inhabitants are like reflections and food.
Because the mirror and the vessel are always one, there is no subject-object distinction; because the reflections and the food are always different, they are said to be "distinctly present."

Thus, within the rational nature, names, and contemplative practice, there already exists the non-dual characteristic of the mutual dependence between the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vyavasthāna*).

To cite these three stages is identical to the previous passage; while the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested, the essence remains unverified and one is still deluded regarding what is called "characteristic"—that is, such is the characteristic of the Buddha-dharma realm.
Therefore, the causes and effects of self and others mutually encompass one another;
the causes and effects of one's own mind and the causes and effects of the Buddhas and sentient beings are constantly uninterrupted.
Yet, although sentient beings have not yet manifested the fruit within the principle, everything without exception is none other than the wondrous realm of Vairocana.

Question: Since this and the previous passage concerning the "nature of reality" (*dharmatā*) and so forth already establish the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*śāśana-śāsita*), how does it differ?

Answer: The former passage exclusively clarifies that the nature is inherently complete (*li-jù*); the present passage points universally to the phenomenal manifestation (*shì-zào*). This is precisely the "wondrous realm. As the *Jinbi* (The Golden Needle) states:
"Sentient beings themselves give rise to divergent views regarding the Buddha’s environment and inhabitants."

However, one must further understand that while the essence of the Buddha-dharma is not pervasive, it is pervasive; and while the rational nature of sentient beings is not restricted, it is restricted.

That the essence of the Dharma is not pervasive yet is said to be pervasive refers to its realization; that the rational nature is not restricted yet is said to be restricted follows from the perspective of deluded sentiment.

Question: If the meaning of restriction is acceptable, why is the Dharma not pervasive? Answer: Since the principle transcends the hundred negations, how could there be anything pervasive? This is because [the mind] follows delusion.
When awakening to phenomena, one speaks of the two ends as being distinguished; yet how could the non-dual nature ever be momentarily different?
Unchanging from beginning to end, there is no obstruction between the Great and the Small.

This is explained by distinguishing between sentient beings and Buddhas: while the Buddhas' dharma-body, which transforms others, remains unchanged from beginning to end, sentient beings [themselves]...

The principle of the nature of reality remains unchanged from beginning to end of practice, such that both the Great and the Small, as well as the environment and its inhabitants (*niṣyanda* and *sattva*), are entirely without mutual obstruction.
Since the principle of cause and effect is identical, how can there be any distinction between the environment and its inhabitants?

Because it is taught [in this manner], I shall briefly set it aside for now.
Since even the body is said to be "no-body," speech is certainly not speech; the wheels of body and mouth are equal to that of the mind.
As clarified above, the [Buddha] should be understood as the Dharmakāya, which is already integrated; provisional means have all become reality, and these are merely what has been taught.
Since Rong has not yet clarified that the capacity to speak is no different [from the speaker], he now uses the body as an analogy for speaking and the two as an analogy for the intent;
when all three are equal, it is only then called "non-duality.
Mind and form are as one, transforming through mutual resonance without deliberation.
Since the three karmas are themselves the Dharma, and since the single suchness transforms as the Dharma, there is no need for deliberation.
Constantly abiding in profound stillness at the ultimate limit, one acts in accordance with the capacities of beings.
Since the Dharma and its transformation occur simultaneously, one joyfully responds without fail.

Is it not the case that the hundred realms are one mind, and that within each realm there is nothing that is not the three karmas? Since even a single thought-moment contains the three karmas, how could they be different?
This reveals that the non-duality of the three karmas on the level of the fruit originally derives from the fact that within the cause, the hundred realms are already one mind.

Since the realms have no distinct dharmas—being merely the combination of the environment and the sentient beings—the three karmas exist only within the primary retribution (the sentient being). Thus, even the realms themselves are fused into one.
How could karma be fixed as three?
Since the function of the fruit is unimpaired, the cause must correspond to the fruit. If one believes in cause and effect, one will know that the three secrets are inherently present.
If one believes that the causal mind possesses the functional power of the fruit, one will know that the phenomena of the three secrets rely upon this inherent basis. If...
Although the meaning is not impaired by the absence of the two characters "cause" and "effect" below the word "faith," the phrasing appears incomplete.
Because the three karmas of the hundred realms are all [identical to] emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, they are appropriately termed as being universally responsive as the fruit.
When the merit of the three contemplations is perfected, the functions of the hundred realms are manifested.
Each and every responsive form and each and every spoken sound is fully endowed with the three karmas of the hundred realms.

Although only the responsive forms and sounds are mentioned without explicitly naming the mind, this is because the body and speech are the manifestations through which one responds to sentient beings.
Therefore, what was stated above—that "one should go everywhere as is appropriate"—is precisely the meaning of the mind-wheel discerning the capacities of beings.
This is what is meant by "transformation further producing transformation.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* clarifies that the nine kinds of great dhyāna, the bodhisattva’s attainment of the Way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and so forth, are all contained therein.

Within the sixth category of all-practice dhyāna (*sarvakāra-dhyāna*), there is the dhyāna of the transformation of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa-nirmāṇa-dhyāna*), which refers to creating a transformation after having already manifested one.
The *Xuanyi* states: "Because it does not require deliberate mental effort (*manasikāra*), it is called 'indeterminate'."
Therefore, within a single thought-moment of the ordinary mind, there already exists the ocean-like array of the three mysteries of the rational nature (*ri-sei*).

What was previously stated—that the cause must correspond to the fruit—clarifies the fundamental essence of all Buddhas; what is now stated—that the ordinary mind of a single thought-moment [possesses this nature]—directly demonstrates the inherent virtue of sentient beings.
This is subsumed as the substance of contemplation (*kan-tai*), and the same applies to all other gates. When students encounter these texts, they should reflect upon them accordingly.

Regarding the three mysteries of the profound and essential rationality, it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* contains the body of the Tathāgata sitting cross-legged within the greed, anger, and ignorance of all sentient beings;
this statement is very familiar, yet few understand it. Lingwei Xiaoliang said:
"Within the midst of birth and death, there fundamentally exists the true spirit, the body of the Buddha, in which the myriad virtues are fully present."
Yet, being shrouded by afflictions, if one can sever these delusions, the Buddha-body manifests spontaneously. Zhanran, citing ancient views to refute [this position], said:
"If one says that the fruit of Buddhahood already exists within the bodies of sentient beings, this implies that there is an effect within the cause, dung within food, or a child within a young girl.
Such a view shows that the lecturer has not mastered the meaning of 'inherently complete' (*yuanju*)."
Frequently, there are discourses on "transcending flavors" that, when pointing toward the inherent goodness of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), claim that the two adornments are already manifest;

yet when pointing toward the existence of evil nature, they claim that the three poisons persist eternally. Such calculations do not transcend the path of self-arising; how are they different from the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*)?
As these transmitted practices spread like creeping vines, the damage is beyond remedy. One must know that the ocean-like marks of the three mysteries are themselves inconceivable (*acintya*).
The wondrous function of liberation manifests universally upon the fruit; even when sought through the four logical possibilities (*catuskoṭi*), it cannot be found.
How much less can the characteristics possessed within the causal stage be described? This is because the essence of the mind of ignorance is itself clarity.

Since there already exists the nature of the wondrous function of liberation, its existence is not a substantial existence, and its non-existence is not a nihilistic non-existence. Although it has not yet taken form when examined, it...
If you practice this, you may seek to understand its principle by consulting the passage on the three metaphors for the inconceivable object of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
"A single atom of retributive form is identical in its fundamental principle to Vairocana."
The three mysteries are the function of Vairocana, and Vairocana is the essence of the three mysteries; mind and form are raised in tandem, for the two must necessarily coexist.
"A single speck of dust is retribution-form"—this refers to the most subtle aspect of bodily karma.
Since the body must necessarily involve speech, the three karmas are all sublime. Master Zhao said: "How distant is the Sage? To embody him is to become spirit."
Only then can it be called the "three non-differentiations," which is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and others;
for transforming others by means of oneself necessarily employs the three karmas.
As for the ninth, the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real: the great wisdom of equality constantly contemplates the dharma-realm.
The statement that "the *yǒngluò* (necklace) is equal" means that the two wisdoms of the provisional (*quán*) and the real (*shí*) illuminate simultaneously.
"Dharmadhātu" refers to the realm of the provisional and the real illuminated by these two wisdoms.

If one follows other texts where the real illuminates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional illuminates the conventional (*prajñapti*), then the three dharmas constitute the realm. However, according to the following passage, which posits nine provisional and one real, it refers to the provisional.
Within the provisional, one distinguishes between the provisional and the real; within emptiness, it belongs to that which is neither provisional nor real.
Thus, only these ten dharmas are taken as the boundary, because they directly correspond to the capacities of those currently to be converted.
Furthermore, by virtue of the principle of nature, there are nine provisional [realms] and one real [realm], yet that reality itself comprises nine realms, and the provisional is likewise so.

Because the ten suchnesses of the nine realms all transform from the true and eternal, they are called "provisional"; because the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm all accord with the Middle Way, it is called "real.
Since the ten realms are mutually inclusive, it is said that the real again contains the nine realms, and so forth.
The provisional and the real are mutually interfused; within a single thought-moment of the hundred realms, they are indivisible.
This corresponds to the passage below which states that the single principle is neither provisional nor real, existing spontaneously and eternally as it is.
Regarding the provisional and the real:
the ultimate fruit arises from acceding to the single principle of the fundamental source; thus, it is neither provisional nor real, yet it is both provisional and real.

This gate derives its name from the teaching spoken; the characteristics of the provisional and the real must be distinguished in relation to the capacities of sentient beings and the establishment of the teachings for them.

According to what is clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the teaching for humans and devas is expounded in contrast to the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), while the four teachings are expounded in contrast to the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, if the *Sijiao yi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states that the Tripitaka Teaching clarifies worldly generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, this refers to the teaching for humans and devas.

Moreover, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says that humans and devas are also subsumed within the Tripitaka Teaching. Thus, in terms of the capacities of sentient beings (*yogya*), these constitute the nine provisional [teachings].
The one reality, when considered in terms of the provisional teachings, is precisely the three provisional means and the one reality.

This is just as previously explained: through the sovereign mastery of the mind-wheel, one causes the body and speech to respond to the capacities of both the provisional and the real; thus, the three karmas are in accord with the provisional and the real in a single thought-moment.
Since there is no movement away from the provisional and the real, how could their application ever be separated or differentiated?
Since the speaker is one and the same, how can what is spoken differ?
When speaking in contrast, they are designated as "expedient" (upāya) and "real" (bhūta); when established in terms of the person, they are named "True" (tathatā) and "Responsive" (nirmāṇa).
Expediency is spoken of in relation to the Responsive Body, while reality is named the True Body; yet the True is not separate from the Responsive, for the Responsive is itself the True.
The principle of the three karmas is identical in that the provisional and the real are in profound harmony.
What was stated above—that they bestow [benefits] while remaining unmoved—clarifies the mutual identity of the provisional and the real;

what is said here regarding their "identical principle" and "profound harmony" reveals that these two dharmas are simultaneously negated. Were it otherwise, the wording would become redundant and cumbersome.
This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas.
Although it applies to all three karmas, it is precisely through verbal discourse that this Dharma’s subtlety is realized.
Regarding the gate of the non-duality of the ten types of recipients being moistened: the nature of phenomena is fundamentally endowed with both the provisional and the real.
The provisional and the real are also discussed in terms of the ten realms. Why is this? This section encompasses the retinues and their benefits;

the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) clarifies that four types of retinues obtain seven kinds of benefits. Are these four types not the capacities of the ten realms? Are these seven kinds not also the benefits for the ten realms?
These capacities and these benefits are inherent within the nature of all things. Question: Regarding the four miserable destinies...

What is the benefit? The answer is: there is benefit in the cause through the destruction of evil, and benefit in the fruit through the departure from suffering; this is as explained in the *Xuánwén*.
Whether it be provisional or real, these are due to beginningless perfuming (*vāsanā*); yet, in terms of principle, the provisional and the real are eternally equal.
The meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is fully contained within the *Awakening of Faith*. It states:
"Just as in the world, a garment has no fragrance in reality, yet because it is perfumed by incense, it comes to have a fragrance; so too is it with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The pure dharma of True Suchness has no defilement in reality, but because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of defilement arises. There is no [defilement] therein.
It clarifies that although defiled phenomena are in reality devoid of pure karma, because they are perfumed by True Suchness (tathatā), a pure function arises.
What was previously termed the "inherent possession of the provisional and the real" refers precisely to True Suchness and ignorance (avidyā).

Although these two dharmas possess only two names and no dual substance, and although they inherently possess the nature of the provisional and the real, in reality they lack the characteristics of the provisional and the real. Now...
Regarding the phrase "beginningless perfuming" and so forth: this refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the nine provisional forms of ignorance arise; because it is perfumed by True Suchness, the one ultimate reality arises.

Although these two meanings both involve internal perfuming, they must rely upon external perfuming to achieve fulfillment. The treatise clarifies that the perfuming of defiled phenomena proceeds through delusion.
The six sense objects as external conditions perfume the pure dharmas, while Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends serve as internal conditions;

thus, through these two types of conditioning—internal and external—there have been no sentient beings since beginningless time who have not thereby developed capacities for the provisional and the real.
Although these capacities differ, their underlying principle is fundamentally non-dual.
"Encountering the opportune time, it becomes habituation, supported by practice and vows.
This clarifies that since the growth of perfuming is said to be "supported by practice and vows," this specifically indicates the meaning of external perfuming.
If there were no fundamental cause, even cultivation would be in vain; that one encounters cultivation and becomes distinct from oneself is not due to a difference in nature.

The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "Because it is internally possessed, others are ultimately able to cultivate it. Thus, when observing what is cultivated, one sees only the principle-possessed (*liju*).

If one observes the principle-possessed, then one recognizes that True Suchness (*tathatā*) constantly cultivates what is internally possessed. In the various treatises and scriptural paths, this point is not seen.
Although it is true that seeds are established through internal and external perfuming, one fails to understand the meaning of "newly perfumed" versus "originally existing.

Therefore, [the claim that] seeds are merely like the primordial darkness (*āṇḍakośa*)—what is the intention behind the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary)? Is this not intended as a refutation of the teachings in the *Awakening of Faith*?
Answer: What kind of words are these, seeking to disparage [the text]? Have you not heard what the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "The dharma-nature is not [afflicted] by delusions"?
Because defilement is not purified by the True [Nature], the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is not the support (*āśraya*). That which is called the "support" is the *ālayavijñāna*.

It is free from extinction, yet it intensely sustains all seeds. Furthermore, the Vijñaptimātra school asserts that *tathatā* (suchness) is without cognition or awakening, being quiescent and unchanging;
they speak only of the arising and ceasing of the seeds of the eight consciousnesses. Moreover, the Hīnayāna...
The Sautrāntika school also maintains the doctrine of the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) of seeds; that which the Master [Yogācāra] refutes is precisely this.
Since the *Awakening of Faith* speaks of the mind of arising and ceasing based upon the Tathāgatagarbha, how could it be identical to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*? Both [schools] have erred.
Furthermore, one must understand that among the various treatises, some state that True Suchness (*tathatā*) gives rise to phenomena, while others speak of the *alaya*.

All dharmas produced by causes and conditions are in accordance with the intent of the *siddhānta* (established tenets) to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings. If one were to focus exclusively on the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), how could one establish the two kinds of emptiness?

Therefore, the *Zhi guan* states: "Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna internally possessed clear and penetrating insight, yet externally they adapted to the exigencies of the times, each relying on provisional means according to the occasion.
Yet today, there are those who transmit the teachings of the Mountain Gate (the Tiantai school) who stubbornly cling to the [Yogācāra] doctrine of existence and disparage the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
To believe that the Master lacked perfect understanding—how lamentable this is!

Moreover, while his doctrine of the dharmadhātu’s perfect fusion and endowment with all virtues—that True Suchness (tathatā) accords with conditions—is indeed profound, it does not yet compare to Tiantai’s detailed demonstration of the nature of both good and evil as inherently complete within reality.
Furthermore, it is similar to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which remains particularly obscure regarding the universal principle, unlike the stages elucidated in the *Mohe zhiguan*.

The Master of Treatises [Zhiyi] maintained that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) sustains both the true and the false, and that since the true and the false depend upon this nature, the mind inherently possesses all phenomena.
Is this not also what Xianshou, Qingliang, and others have taught? Jingxi said:
"The merit of propagating the Dharma and benefiting others does not compensate for the fault of violating the Dharma and slandering others; let later generations be cautious."
Although their nature is without distinction, they must rely on illusion to manifest.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Though one knows that illusory elephants, horses, and various other objects have no reality, their forms are visible.
The four types of illusions used as metaphors in the following passage are all identical to this.
The illusory capacity is the stimulus, the illusory response is the resonance,
the illusory manifestation is the appearance, and the illusory preaching is the arrival.
The capacity that can respond and the beings to be transformed are neither provisional nor ultimate.
Now, when one is able to respond by expounding the provisional and real teachings, those being transformed obtain the benefits of both the provisional and the real;

these are all established based upon the two conditions of defilement and purity. Since defilement and purity are like an illusion, so too are the provisional and the real. Thus, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states:
"If one takes the realization of principle as the standard, then that principle is neither provisional nor real; not even a single dharma is seen."

However, because the nature is inherently complete—being neither provisional nor real—it constitutes the capacity for both the provisional and the real; likewise, the Buddha, as the fruition, is also complete in nature—being neither provisional nor real—and thus acts as the response to both the provisional and the real.
The jewel is neither water nor fire, yet water and fire arise from conditions; the principle is neither provisional nor real, yet the provisional and the real follow according to sentient beings.
The objects and the capacity respond in mutual accord.
Since the objects internally permeate and the capacity is activated, the response immediately externally permeates and accords with it;
this is as stated in the "Gate of Self and Other" regarding the non-deviation between aspiration and arrival. Some versions read "accordance-response" (qiying), which is an error.
The bodies and lands are without partiality, being identical to the eternal *sāmbhogika-kāya* (constant tranquil light), wherein there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The bodies of the ten realms are all the Dharma-realm, and the substance of the three lands is entirely identical to the tranquil light;
since both the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher are thus, it is said they are "without partiality."
Therefore, one should know that the three thousand realms are co-present within the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), and are no different from the three thousand realms of the Buddha’s mind-ground.

Please understand these three thousand realms of the mind-ground through the aforementioned principle that they are neither provisional nor real; thus, the three thousand realms are vaguely perceived as being inherent within consciousness.
The *Guanxin lun shu* (Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) states: "If one were to definitively claim that a single thought-moment contains all phenomena..."
This Tathāgatagarbha is identical to the Kāpila heretics' calculation that the effect pre-exists within the cause;

if one were to rigidly maintain that the mind originally lacks the myriad dharmas and that they only exist through cultivation, this is identical to the Ulūka heretics' calculation that the effect does not exist within the cause.
Even to say that hearing that the mind is endowed with the myriad dharmas is the Tathāgatagarbha is likewise [a misconception].
This means that those who, like a bag of sand, claim that when the mind hears there are no myriad dharmas, are like the horns of a rabbit;
such people are forever clinging to false views, so how can one discuss the Way with them?
The four subtle elements (mahābhūta) are identical in essence, whether provisional or ultimate, and equal in their benefit.

Now, the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*) within a single patch of earth give rise to various plants and trees; though the plants and trees differ, the four subtle elements remain fundamentally the same.
This serves as a metaphor for how the three thousand realms arise from a single principle: though the provisional and the real are distinct, the three thousand realms are not different.

Since they are named after receiving nourishment, this analogy is employed here. [Question: In the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the four subtle elements were used as a metaphor for the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*); why is it now used as a metaphor for this?
Regarding the "three thousand" mentioned here, this is identical in principle to the three virtues, the three truths, and the three thousand [realms] discussed in the preceding text.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real;
because the Dharma is preached, beings receive its moistening benefit.
Therefore, through each of these ten gates, one universally enters into form and mind, and even unto the moisture of sensation; it is thus throughout.

The essential pivot of these ten gates fully prepares the contemplation of the mind, wherein contemplation acts as the means of penetration and the mind is that which is penetrated—this is precisely the intention behind the Master’s establishment of these gates.
How could he have merely indulged in lofty talk of non-duality or empty discourse on the three thousand realms, while leaving form and mind...
Regarding the phrase "naturally flowing therein," the preceding exposition stated that each and every gate is examined by means of the six stages of realization (*liu ji*).
One should know, therefore, that this entry is universal and not restricted to the highest stage alone;
thus, the ten wonders (*shimiao*) are of one principle from beginning to end.
The profundity discussed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) is indeed sublime; however, it does not yet take the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" as its guiding principle.

Therefore, I shall now describe these ten gates based on the passage concerning the inconceivable realm and the three thousand realms of the three truths within the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation).
Since the single principle pervades all that is encompassed by these ten gates, and since these gates themselves subsume the sublime, they ensure that the beginning and the end are unified.
"One thread runs through them all.

Just as the objective realm is inherently endowed with the three [natures], understanding arises based on principle; thus it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Wisdom guides understanding, and understanding accords with practice;
practice accords with principle.

Since the objects (*viṣaya*) already possess three [aspects], the understanding that guides practice must necessarily possess six; because the six [aspects] arise from the three objects, it is said that "practice and understanding accord with reality.

Although the three factors correspond and are not different, they are differentiated as distinct; thus, levels of depth and shallowness are provisionally established to distinguish between them and avoid confusion.

Although the objects, wisdoms, and practices are subtly in accord from beginning to end, because there are degrees of depth and shallowness in wisdom and practice, the stages possess distinctions of high and low.
While they differ temporarily when viewed through phenomena (*dharma*), they are eternally identical when based on principle (*tattva*). Thus it is said: "The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states:

'In the equal Dharma-realm, one does not even discuss awakening or non-awakening; how then could one distinguish between shallow and deep? Once it can be discussed whether there is awakening or non-awakening...'"
What prevents one from discussing the relative shallowness and depth [of realization]?
The three dharmas are simply the three aspects of realizing that principle.

The subtle manifestation of the three dharmas is precisely the three sublime modes (*trividha-yāna*); their development belongs primarily to the ultimate stage, while they also extend secondarily to the provisional stages.
True. In the five chapters that follow, the three dharmas give rise to their function.
Among the five wondrous aspects—such as resonance and so forth—the first three are precisely the arising of function, while the latter two are that which is reached by this function.
Furthermore, among the three dharmas, the Dharma-body is the essence of the function of Prajñā, and liberation is the function of the essence.

Moreover, within Prajñā, there are two types of wisdom: provisional and ultimate; ultimate wisdom takes the true principle as its essence, while provisional wisdom takes the discernment of phenomena as its function.
Since the three dharmas are established as the three thousand in a single thought—namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—they possess efficacy.
This restates that the three dharmas of the beginning and end of the ten profundities are all accomplished through contemplating the nature of the mind; thus they possess efficacy.
"Accomplishment" means proceeding from cause to fruit, wherein the cause effects both self-transformation and the transformation of others.

If one understands that the fundamental and manifested traces of the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are not remote within a single thought-moment, then the ten gates are restated so that the practice of contemplation may be recognized.
This practice of contemplation consists of the ten objects and the ten vehicles; although the ten objects differ, they all take the single thought-moment as their object.
One should know that although the ten vehicles (daśayāna) differ, they are all manifested through the three dharmas;

without the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna-miao*) cannot be established, and without *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), the excellence of practice (*xing-miao*) cannot be established. It is within these ten gates that both are demonstrated together.
Furthermore, if one has not examined the *Xuanyi*, one will not know what is subsumed within the ten gates; nor, if one has not sought out *Zhiguan*, [will one understand their application].

Failing to comprehend what these ten gates encompass, I have now re-expressed them so that those who seek to investigate both sides may catch a glimpse of their profound depths by reading but a few sheets of text and beholding the mysteries of these two treatises.
Liang Su said: "Those who seek pearls by questioning shadows are like the *wangxiang* spirit;
their efforts in seeking the truth are truly not diligent."
Since the title at the beginning is thus, it can be understood that the specific passages are subsumed under the general title.
The title is the general [heading] and the scriptural text constitutes the specific [content].

Since one takes those specific passages to discuss this general meaning, one may employ this general meaning to correspond with the specific text; thus, although the sentences and phrases merely provide a rough division of chapters and sections.
For there is a general profound meaning that encompasses the specific details; thus, the *Wenju ji* states:
"The reason why the title must not be explained in a superficial manner is that the principle of providing a separate explanation beneath the title is no easy matter.

The preceding introduction has already used the 'traces' (*ji*) as an analogy for the 'source' (*ben*), and used the names as an analogy for the four meanings, thereby completing the exposition. Therefore, it concludes: "Since the primary title is thus..."
*Commentary on the Text of the Ten Non-Dual Gates* (End).
From the winter of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, while residing at the Shìshì Aranya in Qiántáng, I produced this private commentary following the lectures.
It was completed in the eighth month of the autumn of the fourth year of the Huángyù era at the Cǎotáng in Xīxī, Wúxīng, at the request of my disciples.
The diligent editor has re-collated and finalized this once more; those who read these annotations may distinguish between the new and the old.
